title: The Recorded Voice
twist: The voice you hear in your head isn't the one other people hear. The 'weird' recording is the accurate one — the voice in your head has extra deep sound carried through bone.
briefing: Malik, 14, records a podcast episode for his English class. When he plays it back his voice sounds higher and thinner — 'that's not me!' His friends listen and say it sounds exactly like him.
question: Which voice is the real Malik — the one in his head or the one on the recording?

clues.title: Thin on playback
clues.text: On the recording his voice sounds higher and thinner than it does when he speaks. He thinks the deep part of his voice is missing.
clues.shows: his recorded voice missing the deep sound he usually hears

visual.unit: how deep it sounds to him, speaking → playback

clues.title: Friends say it's spot on
clues.text: Three friends listen and all agree the recording sounds exactly like Malik. Nothing seems odd to them.
clues.shows: the recording matching what other people hear

clues.title: Fingers in his ears
clues.text: He talks with his fingers in his ears and his voice sounds louder and boomier, even though less sound can get in through the air.
clues.shows: sound reaching his ears from inside his head, not through the air

clues.title: Everyone hates their own
clues.text: The whole class says their own recording sounds strange to them. But their friends' recordings sound completely normal on the same phone.
clues.shows: it happening to everyone, but only for their own voice

hypotheses.text: The phone's microphone is cheap and changes his voice.
hypotheses.flaw: His friends say the recording sounds exactly like him, and everyone else's recordings sound normal on the same phone.

hypotheses.text: He has a cold, so his voice was different that day.
hypotheses.flaw: Everyone in class felt the same about their own recording, and he doesn't sound different to his friends.

hypotheses.text: Malik hears his own voice two ways — through the air and through the bones of his skull, which carry the deep sounds best. The recording only catches the air route, which is what everyone else hears.
Hearing yourself played back makes you nervous, so you imagine it sounds wrong.
hypotheses.flaw: Nerves can't explain why plugging his ears makes his voice boomier — that is a real change in the sound reaching his ears.

prediction.prompt: Across the pitches in Malik's voice, from low to high, how much extra loudness does the 'through the bone' route add?

second.question: If Malik plugs his ears while talking, does his voice sound deeper or less deep to him?

transfer.context: When Inés eats crunchy chips, the crunching sounds really loud to her — but her friend across the table can barely hear it.
options: Inés's chips are crunchier than her friend's.
The crunch travels through the bones of Inés's jaw and skull straight to her ears, a route her friend's ears don't get.
transfer.retryHint: What happened to Malik's voice when sound could only reach his ears from inside his head?
transfer.explanation: Just like Malik's voice, the crunch reaches Inés's ears through the bones of her own head as well as through the air. Her friend only gets the quiet air route — the same reason a recording of your voice sounds 'thin' to you.

takeaway: You hear your own voice through the air and through the bones of your head, which add deep tones. A recording catches only the air — so the strange-sounding playback is how everyone else hears you.
